sources.citation: Faust, Noam. 2023. Metrically-conditioned syncope in Strict CV metrics. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 8(1): 1-29. doi:10.16995/glossa.8764
sources.quote: Metrically-conditioned syncope in Tonkawa affects both long and short vowels. For short ones, sequences of two light syllables (underlined in (24)) are not allowed. Long vowels, in turn, may surface anywhere in the word, except after initial light syllables. In this configuration, the initial light syllable is stressed and the long vowel is shortened (compare (24d,f) to (24a–c, e)).

sources.citation: Gouskova, Maria. 2007. The reduplicative template in Tonkawa. Phonology 24(3): 367-396. doi:10.1017/S0952675707001261
sources.quote: According to Hoijer's description, "Tonkawa utterances consist of a succession of more or less evenly stressed syllables" (1946:292). This characterization is consistent with iterative footing. Although Hoijer does not mark stress on his examples, further evidence from the distribution of long vowels (see (2)) points to trochaic feet. [...] if Tonkawa has trochaic H́, H́L, and ĹL feet, the context of shortening is simple to state: it applies to the vowel that ends up in the weak branch of a trochaic foot. [fn. 4:] Hoijer is not very definite about the position of primary stress, but it is not crucial to the present discussion. [fn. 14:] Hoijer (1946) suggests that disyllables have somewhat stronger stress on the ultima, so the initial syllable may not be footed, or may form only a degenerate foot. [fn. 23:] we do not have a detailed record of stress in Tonkawa.

sources.quote: Quotes Hoijer 1946:292 'Tonkawa utterances consist of a succession of more or less evenly stressed syllables'; fn.50 quotes verbatim the disyllable-final / polysyllable-penult sentence and conjectures the disyllable remark may reflect apocope words like notox 'hoe'; 'Hoijer's description of stress is not detailed enough to deduce whether Tonkawa has iambic or trochaic stress' (she infers trochaic footing from vowel shortening).
